fixes.explanation: Himself. Verse 14 says the priest would claim for himself whatever the meat fork brought up. The servant plunged that three-pronged fork into the pot, and whatever came up on it was claimed by the priest. I'd say that's a pretty handy setup for him.

Good thought, since it was a sacrifice, but that's not what verse 14 says. The priest would claim for himself whatever the meat fork brought up. The fork went in the pot, and what it brought up was claimed by the priest. The altar isn't mentioned in that verse.

Contempt. Verse 17 says, “…they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt.” That offering belonged to the LORD, and the text names exactly how these young men treated it. Contempt means looking down on something.
Fear isn't the word the text gives, friend. Verse 17 says, “…they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt.” Eli's sons had no regard for the LORD (1 Samuel 2:12). Contempt is the word for it.

A belt is a nice guess, friend, but nothing is getting cinched in this verse. Verse 19 says his mother would make him a little robe each year and bring it to him. Hannah, Samuel's mother, made it herself. A robe is the one thing the verse names.

Not this time, friend. Eli says the opposite: “it is not a good report I hear circulating among the LORD’s people.” He's heard what people are saying about his sons, and I think he's not happy about it. I think that's a hard thing for a father to say to his own sons.

That's a kind thought, but Eli doesn't say it. In verse 25 he asks, “…if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?” He doesn't answer with family, or anyone else. The question is left hanging.

Not here, friend. Verse 25 says, “But they would not listen to their father, since the LORD intended to put them to death.” Eli warned them, and they would not listen. It's a heavy verse, and the text doesn't soften it.

That's right. The text says, “But they would not listen to their father, since the LORD intended to put them to death.” (1 Samuel 2:25). Eli spoke up, and his sons would not listen. It's a heavy moment.

Priest. In verse 28 the LORD says, “…out of all the tribes of Israel I selected your father to be My priest…” He selected Eli's father out of all the tribes of Israel, so I think that was a big honor. That makes what happens next even harder to hear.
The servants did plenty of grabbing, but they're not who the LORD names here. He tells Eli, “You have honored your sons more than Me…” (1 Samuel 2:29). The word is sons.

Yes. The LORD says, “They will both die on the same day.” (1 Samuel 2:34). Hophni and Phinehas are Eli's two sons, and this is the sign He gives Eli. I think this one hurts, so I'll just say it plainly and move on.

Priestly. Verse 36 has them pleading, “Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread.” Everyone left in Eli's house will come and bow down for a piece of silver or a morsel of bread. Priestly is the word they use.

Fancy guess, friend, but nobody's asking for a crown. Verse 36 has them pleading, “Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread.” They're asking for a priestly office, not a royal one.
